stem: A 62-year-old man has typical exertional chest pain relieved by rest and GTN. Investigations confirm stable angina with preserved LV function. Which combination is the MOST appropriate initial medical management?
options: Aspirin, statin, beta-blocker and sublingual GTN as required
Warfarin, statin and calcium-channel blocker
Aspirin alone with GTN, add statin only if total cholesterol is raised
ACE inhibitor, diuretic and digoxin
Ranolazine and nicorandil as first-line therapy
explanation: Stable angina: antiplatelet (aspirin), high-intensity statin, rate-limiting antianginal (beta-blocker first-line if no contraindication) plus GTN PRN for breakthrough.
pearl: Four pillars: aspirin + statin + beta-blocker + GTN.
trap: Forgetting the statin - it is part of angina management, not just for high cholesterol.

stem: A 68-year-old hypertensive man has sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back. BP is 190/105 in the right arm and 150/90 in the left. ECG is non-diagnostic. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: CT angiography of the aorta via emergency transfer
Troponin to exclude myocardial infarction before proceeding
Transthoracic echocardiogram in the practice
Oral antihypertensive and review in the morning
Exercise stress test
explanation: Tearing pain to the back with inter-arm BP differential is classic dissection. Time-critical: emergency transfer for CT angiography (or TOE if unstable). Troponin and stress testing are dangerous delays.
pearl: BP difference between arms or new aortic regurgitation murmur: think dissection.
trap: Anchoring on troponin/ECG because the pain is chest pain.

stem: A 70-year-old woman has breathlessness, orthopnoea and ankle oedema. BNP is raised and an echocardiogram shows HFrEF (EF 35%). She is euvolaemic. Which single management plan is MOST appropriate?
options: Start an ACE inhibitor (or ARNI), beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor as tolerated
Furosemide alone as long-term therapy
Digoxin first-line to improve ejection fraction
ACE inhibitor only once symptoms worsen
Referral for transplant assessment before any medication
explanation: HFrEF quadruple therapy (ACEi/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) reduces mortality and is started early and titrated. Diuretics manage congestion but do not alter prognosis.
pearl: Four disease-modifying drugs in HFrEF; diuretics are for volume, not mortality.
trap: Digoxin - symptom/rate drug, not first-line mortality therapy.

stem: A 54-year-old man attends with BP 214/128 on repeated reading. He has a mild headache but no chest pain, no neurological signs, and urinalysis is clear. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Commence or adjust oral antihypertensives and arrange same-day medical review
IV antihypertensive in the practice
Increase his existing amlodipine and review in 2 weeks
Recheck in 1 week with no medication change
Observation only as he is asymptomatic
explanation: Severe asymptomatic hypertension (no target-organ damage features) is managed with prompt oral therapy and same-day review. IV therapy and ED are for hypertension emergencies with organ damage.
pearl: Emergency = high BP plus organ damage (chest pain, neuro signs, pulmonary oedema).
trap: IV bolus antihypertensives causing precipitous drops - or waiting weeks unreviewed.

stem: A 32-year-old woman has BP 165/100 despite three antihypertensives. Potassium is 3.1, sodium 139, and she is not on a diuretic. Which investigation is MOST likely to reveal the diagnosis?
options: Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio
Renal artery angiography
24-hour urinary metanephrines
Thyroid function tests
Echocardiogram
explanation: Young onset resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia strongly suggests primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome). The screening test is the aldosterone:renin ratio (ensure interfering drugs reviewed first).
pearl: Resistant + young + low K = screen for secondary causes, starting with ARR.
trap: Jumping to imaging before biochemical screening.

stem: An 83-year-old woman on amlodipine and doxazosin has dizziness on standing and a fall. Lying BP 150/84, standing BP 118/70 with symptoms. What is the MOST useful single intervention?
options: Cease or reduce the doxazosin and give standing-up advice
Add fludrocortisone
Increase the amlodipine dose
Add midodrine
Encourage increased salt and fluid restriction of her evening dose
explanation: Symptomatic postural hypotension: first review culprit drugs (alpha-blockers, vasodilators, diuretics) and give behavioural advice (stand slowly, legs crossed, adequate fluids). Pressor agents are later options.
pearl: Drug review before drug addition in older fallers.
trap: Prescribing a new drug for a drug side-effect.

stem: A 42-year-old man has LDL 6.1 mmol/L, no other risk factors. His brother had an MI at 44 and his father at 49. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Refer to a specialist lipid service for suspected familial hypercholesterolaemia and arrange family cascade screening
Start a statin and review in 12 months
Reassure - it is only relevant once absolute risk exceeds 15%
Start ezetimibe alone
Repeat the lipid profile in 5 years
explanation: LDL >5 mmol/L with a family history of premature CVD suggests familial hypercholesterolaemia: refer for specialist assessment, treat as high risk, and trigger cascade screening of relatives. FH is not risk-calculator-dependent.
pearl: FH bypasses absolute-risk calculation - it is automatically high risk.
trap: Reassuring on the basis of a low calculated 5-year risk score.

stem: A 66-year-old smoker has calf pain walking 200 metres, relieved by standing still. Ankle-brachial index is 0.62. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Supervised walking-exercise program with smoking-cessation support, antiplatelet and statin
Immediate referral for lower-limb bypass surgery
Referral for lumbar sympathectomy
Compression stockings
Rest and elevation of the legs
explanation: Intermittent claudication is managed first with supervised exercise, smoking cessation, antiplatelet and statin therapy. Revascularisation is reserved for critical limb ischaemia or lifestyle-limiting claudication refractory to best medical therapy.
pearl: Supervised exercise + stop smoking beat scalpel for most claudication.
trap: Operating before best medical therapy, or compression (harmful in arterial disease).

stem: A 68-year-old man with permanent AF has resting HR 105 despite monotherapy. He has mild asthma. Which is the MOST appropriate rate-control first-line agent?
options: A cardioselective beta-blocker (e.g., metoprolol or bisoprolol)
Digoxin
Verapamil
Amiodarone
Flecainide
explanation: Beta-blockers (cardioselective) are first-line for AF rate control and safe in most mild asthma (monitor). Digoxin is for sedentary patients or add-on; verapamil an alternative if beta-blocker contraindicated (caution asthma is fine for verapamil actually, but beta-blockers remain first choice). Amiodarone/flecainide are rhythm agents.
pearl: Rate first: beta-blocker; verapamil if beta-blocker truly contraindicated.
trap: Amiodarone for simple rate control - long-term toxicity.

stem: A 19-year-old athlete collapses briefly while sprinting. He reports central chest tightness during training over recent weeks. Examination is normal. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Urgent cardiology referral with echocardiogram for exertional syncope
Reassure - vasovagal syncope is common in the young
Holter monitor organised routinely and review in 6 months
Electroencephalogram
Prescribe a beta-blocker and review in 3 months
explanation: Exertional syncope is a red flag suggesting an arrhythmic or structural cause (HOCM, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy) and mandates urgent cardiology assessment with echo and ECG before resuming sport.
pearl: Exertional syncope is never vasovagal until proven otherwise.
trap: Reassurance - a common and dangerous reflex in young patients.

stem: An 80-year-old man survived an MI 3 months ago. He continues to smoke, takes all his medications, and asks what single measure will reduce his future risk most. What do you advise?
options: Stopping smoking
Doubling his statin dose
Adding a fibrate
Monthly CPAP for nocturnal snoring
Low-dose aspirin increase to 300 mg daily
explanation: Smoking cessation is the single most powerful secondary-prevention intervention post-MI, reducing mortality substantially. No pharmacologic adjustment outperforms quitting in a continuing smoker.
pearl: In a smoker post-MI, quitting beats any tablet change.
trap: Escalating drugs while the modifiable driver is ignored.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has exertional breathlessness and one episode of syncope on exertion. She has an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids with a slow-rising pulse. Echo shows severe aortic stenosis. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Urgent referral for valve intervention assessment (surgical or transcatheter)
Annual echo monitoring only
ACE inhibitor and diuretic as for heart failure
Commence anticoagulation
Exercise program to improve exertional symptoms
explanation: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis (angina, syncope, heart failure) has a poor prognosis without valve replacement; refer urgently for intervention. Vasodilators can precipitate collapse.
pearl: Syncope + AS = urgent; avoid vasodilators.
trap: Treating AS as ordinary heart failure with ACE inhibitors.

stem: A 58-year-old man had a drug-eluting stent inserted after an NSTEMI 2 months ago and takes aspirin plus clopidogrel. He asks how long the clopidogrel must continue. What is the MOST appropriate advice, assuming no high bleeding risk?
options: Continue dual antiplatelet therapy for 12 months in total, then aspirin long-term
Stop the clopidogrel now as the stent is endothelialised
Lifelong clopidogrel plus aspirin
3 months in total is sufficient for all stents
Switch clopidogrel to warfarin at 12 months
explanation: After ACS with DES, standard DAPT duration is around 12 months (individualised for bleeding risk), then lifelong single antiplatelet (aspirin). Premature cessation risks stent thrombosis.
pearl: DAPT 12 months post-ACS; never stop both agents without cardiology advice.
trap: Stopping antiplatelets for minor procedures without coordination.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a prosthetic mitral valve has 2 weeks of fever, night sweats and new splinter haemorrhages. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: At least three sets of blood cultures before any antibiotics, then inpatient antibiotics
Immediate oral amoxicillin in the community
Start empirical IV flucloxacillin today to avoid delay
Repeat inflammatory markers and review next week
Transthoracic echo at the practice
explanation: Suspected endocarditis requires multiple blood cultures before antibiotics (to identify the organism and guide weeks of therapy) plus inpatient management; echo follows.
pearl: Culture first: endocarditis therapy is organism-directed for 4-6 weeks.
trap: Empirical antibiotics destroying the diagnostic yield.

stem: A 28-year-old man has sharp pleuritic chest pain improved by leaning forward. ECG shows saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression. Troponin is mildly raised. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: NSAID plus colchicine for up to 3 months
Immediate coronary angiography for the raised troponin
Antibiotics for presumed myocarditis
Steroids as first-line therapy
Aspirin alone for 1 week
explanation: Acute pericarditis (with or without myopericarditis) is treated with NSAIDs plus colchicine, which reduces recurrence. Steroids are second-line (associated with relapse). Mild troponin rise indicates myopericarditis, not automatic angiography, in a clear pericarditis picture.
pearl: Colchicine halves pericarditis recurrence.
trap: Mild troponin elevation reflexively triggering the ACS pathway.

stem: A 49-year-old man snores heavily, wakes unrefreshed and falls asleep at his desk. BMI 36, BP 152/94, neck 45 cm. Epworth score is 16. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Refer for a sleep study
Trial of mandibular advancement splint
Start modafinil for daytime sleepiness
Nasal steroid spray and review in 6 months
Weight-loss advice alone with no objective testing
explanation: High pre-test probability OSA (STOP-BANG high, Epworth 16, hypertension): confirm severity with a sleep study (home or in-lab) to guide CPAP and cardiovascular risk management. Stimulants treat the symptom, not the disease.
pearl: Sleepy + snoring + hypertensive + obese = study, not guesswork.
trap: Medicating sleepiness without diagnosing the cause.

stem: A 66-year-old smoker has 3 months of right shoulder pain unresponsive to physiotherapy, now with right arm weakness and drooping eyelid. What is the MOST appropriate initial investigation?
options: Chest X-ray today, with urgent respiratory referral if abnormal
MRI of the cervical spine
Shoulder ultrasound
Nerve conduction studies for brachial plexopathy
Trial of pregabalin and review in 4 weeks
explanation: Shoulder pain plus arm wasting with ptosis and miosis in a smoker is a Pancoast tumour (apical lung cancer invading the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain). CXR is the first test, then urgent respiratory referral.
pearl: Pancoast = arm symptoms + Horner syndrome; look at the lung apex.
trap: Managing chronic shoulder pain without imaging in a high-risk smoker.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with acute pleuritic breathlessness 10 days after a hip replacement. She is haemodynamically stable, HR 98, SpO2 93%. Wells score is moderate probability. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: CT pulmonary angiogram without waiting for d-dimer
D-dimer alone, imaging only if positive
Ventilation-perfusion scan in 3 days
Lower-limb ultrasound first
Start therapeutic enoxaparin and observe overnight
explanation: With moderate-to-high pre-test probability, d-dimer cannot rule out PE; go straight to CTPA. D-dimer is only for low probability. She also needs anticoagulation once confirmed (post-operative provoked VTE).
pearl: D-dimer excludes only in low-probability presentations.
trap: A negative d-dimer falsely reassuring in a moderate-probability patient.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with well-controlled asthma is 10 weeks pregnant and asks about her preventer. What is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: Continue her regular ICS (budesonide preferred in pregnancy) - good control protects mother and baby
Stop all asthma medication during the first trimester
Switch the preventer to oral theophylline
Use salbutamol only, as frequently as needed
Commence oral corticosteroids prophylactically
explanation: Untreated asthma in pregnancy is riskier than treated asthma. Continue ICS (budesonide has the best pregnancy data) with reliever as needed. Poor control raises hypoxia and preterm risk.
pearl: Pregnant asthmatics: preventers stay, avoid the trap of stopping inhaled steroids.
trap: Withdrawing preventers and treating only symptoms.

stem: A 70-year-old man with COPD (FEV1 48%) has had two hospital admissions for exacerbations this year. He still smokes. Which intervention is MOST likely to reduce his future admissions and mortality?
options: Pulmonary rehabilitation plus smoking-cessation support
Long-term oral prednisolone
Home oxygen despite adequate saturations
Long-term azithromycin for all patients
Inhaled corticosteroid monotherapy
explanation: Pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise capacity and reduces admissions; smoking cessation is the only intervention that slows decline and improves survival. Steroid tablets are harmful long-term; prophylactic azithromycin is for selected patients.
pearl: Rehab + quitting: the two highest-yield COPD interventions.
trap: Maintenance oral steroids for COPD - delirium, osteoporosis, diabetes.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has a 10-year history of daily purulent sputum, recurrent chest infections and two hospitalisations. She is a lifelong non-smoker. Which investigation will MOST likely establish the diagnosis?
options: High-resolution CT chest
Spirometry with reversibility
Bronchoscopy with lavage
Sputum culture alone
Chest X-ray
explanation: Chronic productive cough with recurrent infections and possible clubbing suggests bronchiectasis; HRCT is the diagnostic standard. Spirometry is often normal or shows non-specific obstruction; plain films are insensitive.
pearl: Daily purulent sputum for years = HRCT.
trap: Labelling it smoker's cough or asthma for a non-smoker.

stem: A 63-year-old smoker has FEV1 58% predicted and FEV1/FVC 0.55, unchanged post-bronchodilator. He has never had respiratory investigations before. What is the MOST appropriate interpretation?
options: spirometry confirms airflow limitation not reversed by bronchodilator - consistent with COPD
Reversible airflow obstruction consistent with asthma
Restrictive lung disease
Normal age-related spirometry
Inconclusive - repeat spirometry in 12 months
explanation: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms persistent airflow limitation, defining COPD; a significant bronchodilator response would instead suggest asthma.
pearl: COPD = post-BD FEV1/FVC <0.70, persisting.
trap: Diagnosing COPD on symptoms alone without spirometry.

stem: A 45-year-old teacher has 3 weeks of paroxysmal coughing fits ending in vomiting, worse at night, afebrile. Her whooping cough immunity has lapsed. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Azithromycin and notify the public health unit
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
No treatment as the infectious period has passed at 3 weeks
Chest X-ray before any antibiotic
Salbutamol and review
explanation: Pertussis is clinical (cough >2 weeks with paroxysms/post-tussive vomiting in an adult): a macrolide within the treatment window reduces transmission, and pertussis is notifiable. Antibiotics rarely change the course at 3 weeks but limit spread.
pearl: Macrolide + notify; vaccinate household contacts per public health advice.
trap: Assuming antibiotics at 3 weeks help the patient - they help the contacts.

stem: A 19-year-old man has 2 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and 5 kg weight loss. Capillary glucose is 21 mmol/L with urine ketones 2+. He is alert. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Same-day transfer to hospital for IV fluids and insulin
Start basal-bolus insulin and review tomorrow in the practice
Start metformin and dietary review this week
Oral fluids and repeat glucose in 4 hours
Refer to a diabetes educator over the next month
explanation: New type 1 diabetes with ketosis risks DKA; same-day hospital assessment with fluids and insulin is mandatory. Oral hypoglycaemics and delays are dangerous.
pearl: Glucose high + ketones = hospital today.
trap: A well-looking young adult masking the urgency of impending DKA.

stem: A 68-year-old woman has a TSH of 0.03 with a normal free T4, persisting on repeat over 6 months, plus new atrial fibrillation risk factors. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Specialist referral for definitive management of subclinical thyrotoxicosis
Reassure and recheck in 12 months
Start carbimazole
Start levothyroxine
No action ever needed for a low TSH with normal T4
explanation: Persistent subclinical hyperthyroidism in an older patient carries AF and bone-loss risk; endocrine referral for consideration of definitive therapy (radioiodine or surgery) is appropriate, with cardiology input for AF.
pearl: Subclinical hyper in older bones and hearts is not benign.
trap: Dismissing a suppressed TSH as trivial when fT4 is normal.

stem: A 52-year-old woman on levothyroxine 100 mcg is started on iron tablets by another doctor and now reports fatigue; her TSH has risen. What is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: Separate levothyroxine and iron by at least 4 hours
Double her levothyroxine dose
Switch all iron intake to afternoon and take thyroid hormone with it
Stop the iron permanently
Take both together with breakfast to improve absorption of each
explanation: Iron (and calcium) markedly reduces levothyroxine absorption, causing rising TSH. Separating doses by 4+ hours (or a different formulation) resolves it without dose escalation.
pearl: Iron and thyroxine in the same stomach = therapeutic failure.
trap: Escalating the dose to overcome an interaction.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with ultrasound-confirmed PCOS has irregular cycles and acne; she is not seeking pregnancy. What is the MOST appropriate first-line management?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pill plus lifestyle changes
Metformin alone
Clomiphene immediately
Anti-androgen cyproterone alone without contraception
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling
explanation: In women not seeking fertility, the combined OCP regulates cycles, treats acne/hirsutism and provides contraception; lifestyle change addresses the metabolic substrate. Metformin is adjunct for metabolic features, not the primary cycle/acne therapy.
pearl: Not seeking pregnancy = COCP first.
trap: Fertility drugs in a woman not trying to conceive - teratogenic and pointless.

stem: A 61-year-old man attends for his annual diabetes review. Which set of assessments constitutes the recommended annual cycle of care?
options: HbA1c, blood pressure, lipids, eGFR and ACR, dilated eye examination, foot risk assessment
HbA1c alone each year with eyes every 5 years
Fasting glucose quarterly and nothing else
Random glucose when symptomatic
HbA1c and lipids only if he feels unwell
explanation: The annual cycle of care for T2DM covers glycaemia, cardiovascular risk factors (BP, lipids), nephropathy screening (eGFR + ACR), retinopathy screening, and foot assessment, plus vaccination and lifestyle review.
pearl: Kidneys (ACR), eyes, feet, BP, lipids, HbA1c - every year.
trap: Tight HbA1c focus while the complications screens lapse.

stem: A 48-year-old insulin-treated truck driver asks about safe driving. What is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: Check glucose before driving; if below 4 mmol/L treat, wait 15 minutes and recheck before driving
Drive only within 30 minutes of eating, without testing
Stop driving permanently once on insulin
Keep sweets in the cab instead of testing
If hypoglycaemic while driving, continue to the next town then stop
explanation: Austroads and diabetes guidance: SMBG before driving for insulin users; hypo <4 = stop safely, treat, wait and recheck before resuming. Also discuss reporting obligations for specified conditions.
pearl: Before the key turns, the glucometer reads.
trap: Treating through the symptoms without rechecking.

stem: A 62-year-old man starts prednisolone 50 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica. Six weeks later he reports thirst and nocturia. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Check glucose/HbA1c - corticosteroids commonly unmask diabetes
Assume it is PMR-related fatigue and increase the prednisolone
Reassure that steroids cannot raise glucose
Start metformin empirically without testing
Reduce steroids to 5 mg to prevent diabetes
explanation: High-dose corticosteroids induce insulin resistance and commonly unmask or worsen diabetes - check BGL/HbA1c when symptoms arise on steroids (usually post-prandial first).
pearl: Steroid hyperglycaemia is typically worst in the afternoon (dose timing).
trap: Blaming the underlying disease instead of its treatment.

stem: A 44-year-old woman with BMI 38 and type 2 diabetes has not achieved target weight with 12 months of structured lifestyle support. She asks about medication. What is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: A GLP-1 receptor agonist may be added to lifestyle therapy for eligible patients, alongside continued diet and activity support
Orlistat is the only option ever available
Weight-loss medication replaces the need for lifestyle measures
Phentermine long-term is standard care
No medication is appropriate once lifestyle has failed
explanation: For patients with obesity (especially with comorbidities) who have not reached goals with lifestyle alone, adjunct pharmacotherapy - GLP-1 agonists for eligible patients - is appropriate, always continued WITH lifestyle measures.
pearl: Drugs augment lifestyle; they never replace it.
trap: Either/or thinking - medication or lifestyle.

stem: A 58-year-old man on long-term NSAIDs reports 3 months of worsening dysphagia to solids and 6 kg weight loss. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Urgent endoscopy for alarm features
Double the proton-pump inhibitor and review in 8 weeks
Barium swallow
Trial of a liquid diet and reassurance
H. pylori stool antigen testing
explanation: Dysphagia plus weight loss in an older patient on NSAIDs are alarm features mandating urgent endoscopy to exclude malignancy - do not empirically escalate acid suppression.
pearl: Dysphagia + weight loss + anaemia + new symptoms over 55 = scope.
trap: Reassuring a red-flag symptom with a PPI trial.

stem: A 32-year-old woman has 2 years of recurring abdominal pain relieved by defaecation, bloating and alternating bowel habit, with no weight loss, anaemia or bleeding. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Positive diagnosis explanation, dietary review including a trial of a low-FODMAP diet with a dietitian
Colonoscopy to exclude malignancy first
Long-term codeine for the pain
Wheat allergy testing
Repeated courses of antibiotics
explanation: Rome IV criteria with absence of red flags supports a positive IBS diagnosis without invasive testing: explanation, dietary management (low-FODMAP, dietitian), symptom-directed therapy.
pearl: IBS is diagnosed positively; the colonoscopy is for red flags.
trap: Investigating indefinitely while never treating.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has iron deficiency and intermittent loose stools. Her sister has coeliac disease. Which testing approach is correct BEFORE any diet change?
options: tissue transglutaminase IgA with a total IgA level, on a gluten-containing diet
tTG IgG alone, sufficient in all cases
HLA typing first for everyone
Start a gluten-free diet and test if symptoms persist
Anti-gliadin antibodies as the screening test of choice
explanation: Screen with tTG-IgA plus total IgA (to detect IgA deficiency causing false negatives), while still eating gluten; diagnosis in adults is confirmed by duodenal biopsy. Anti-gliadin antibodies are obsolete for screening.
pearl: Test on gluten; a gluten-free diet before testing erases the diagnosis.
trap: Empirical gluten-free trial in a first-degree relative - losing the diagnostic window.

stem: A 35-year-old man from a high-prevalence country has a positive HBsAg on screening. LFTs are normal. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Refer for specialist assessment, screen and vaccinate household and sexual contacts, and monitor regularly
Reassure that a positive surface antigen means past resolved infection
Start entecavir immediately in all cases
No follow-up needed while LFTs remain normal
Isolate him from family meals
explanation: HBsAg positivity indicates chronic infection requiring specialist-linked surveillance (cirrhosis/HCC) and contact management (screening and vaccination of household/sexual contacts). Normal LFTs do not exclude active disease.
pearl: HBsAg positive = chronic infection until proven otherwise; protect the family.
trap: Confusing surface antigen (chronic) with surface antibody (immune).

stem: A 46-year-old man with a history of injecting drug use has a positive hepatitis C antibody and detectable RNA. He asks about treatment. What is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: Direct-acting antiviral therapy cures over 95% of patients and is PBS-subsidised; assess fibrosis and treat
Interferon-based therapy remains the standard
Treatment is only for cirrhosis
He must abstain from alcohol for 5 years before treatment is permitted
No treatment exists; monitor LFTs yearly
explanation: All HCV patients should be considered for curative DAAs (>95% sustained virological response, PBS-listed), with fibrosis assessment (and vaccination for hep A/B) beforehand. Injecting-drug history is not an exclusion.
pearl: Hepatitis C is a curable disease - test, link, treat.
trap: Old interferon-era beliefs denying treatment to people who use drugs.

stem: A 61-year-old asymptomatic man returns a positive National Bowel Cancer Screening Program iFOBT. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Refer for colonoscopy
Repeat the iFOBT in 3 months
Start a trial of dietary modification
Faecal occult blood testing on three consecutive days to confirm
CT abdomen as a less invasive alternative
explanation: A positive iFOBT in the screening program mandates colonoscopy - do not repeat the test or substitute imaging. This is the diagnostic step of the program.
pearl: Positive FOBT = scope, not re-test.
trap: Serial FOBTs delaying a cancer diagnosis.

stem: A 63-year-old man has Hb 102 with ferritin 8 and microcytosis, no obvious blood loss. Colonoscopy and gastroscopy are planned. What is the MOST appropriate iron therapy advice once workup is underway?
options: Oral iron continued for 3 months after haemoglobin normalises to replenish stores
Stop iron once Hb reaches the reference range
IV iron routinely before endoscopy
Oral iron only if ferritin remains low after Hb normalises
No iron needed - treat the cause only
explanation: Treat the cause (bidirectional endoscopy in men/postmenopausal women with IDA) AND replace iron; continue oral iron ~3 months beyond Hb normalisation to replete stores. IV iron if intolerant or severe.
pearl: Haemoglobin normalised is not iron repleted - keep going 3 months.
trap: Stopping at normal Hb, guaranteeing early relapse.

stem: A 66-year-old man has 4 months of progressive dysphagia, first to solids then liquids, with 8 kg weight loss. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Urgent endoscopy
Oesophageal manometry
Trial of a proton-pump inhibitor for 8 weeks
Barium swallow as the definitive test
Speech pathology assessment for swallowing therapy
explanation: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss in an older patient is oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise; urgent endoscopy (with biopsy). Manometry is for motility disorders once structural disease is excluded.
pearl: Progressive + weight loss = scope.
trap: PPI trials for an alarm symptom.

stem: A 54-year-old woman has left iliac fossa pain, fever 38.2, and tenderness without peritonism. WCC 16, CRP 90. CT shows uncomplicated acute diverticulitis. She is tolerating fluids. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Oral amoxycillin-clavulanate with clear fluids and early review, ED if worsening
Oral metronidazole alone
Hospital admission with IV antibiotics for all diverticulitis
No antibiotics - resolution is typically uncomplicated without them
Colonoscopy this week
explanation: Uncomplicated diverticulitis in a systemically unwell patient is treated with oral broad-spectrum antibiotics (amoxycillin-clavulanate per eTG), fluid, and safety-netting; complicated disease (peritonism, abscess, obstruction, sepsis) goes to ED. Colonoscopy follows later to exclude missed neoplasia.
pearl: Simple diverticulitis: oral antibiotics + early review; reserve ED for complications.
trap: Missing peritonism or free air that changes everything.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has migraines on 10 days per month affecting work, with depression and poor sleep. Which prophylactic agent best fits her profile?
options: Amitriptyline at night
Propranolol
Verapamil
Pizotifen
Codeine-based analgesia nightly
explanation: At 10 headache days/month, prophylaxis is indicated. Amitriptyline addresses migraine, insomnia and coexisting depression. Choice is comorbidity-tailored; avoid nightly codeine which guarantees medication-overuse headache.
pearl: Prophylaxis at ≥4 migraine days/month; pick the drug that treats a second condition.
trap: Nightly opioids - the highway to medication-overuse headache.

stem: A 70-year-old man describes 20 minutes of left arm weakness and slurred speech yesterday that fully resolved. He feels well today. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Urgent same-day assessment (stroke/TIA clinic or ED)
Routine appointment next week
Reassure as symptoms resolved
CT brain as an outpatient sometime in the next month
Start aspirin and review in 3 months
explanation: TIA carries up to ~10% early stroke risk, highest in the first days: Australian guidance is same-day assessment (ED or rapid-access TIA clinic) for workup and secondary prevention, not watchful waiting.
pearl: Resolved deficit does not mean resolved risk - same-day workup.
trap: Waiting days for a scan and aspirin.

stem: A 25-year-old man had a first unprovoked seizure yesterday. He asks about driving. What is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: Do not drive now; report per the licensing authority's medical reporting process and Austroads guidelines, with return to driving only once the seizure-free requirement is met
He may drive as long as someone accompanies him
Driving is fine because the seizure was a one-off
A one-week break from driving is sufficient
No restrictions apply to the first seizure
explanation: After an unprovoked seizure, driving must cease and the licensing process (with its seizure-free interval requirement) applies; the GP's job is to counsel clearly, document, and fulfil reporting obligations per Austroads and state rules.
pearl: First seizure = no driving; notify and document the advice.
trap: Soft-pedalling the driving conversation - it is a legal and safety duty.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has 18 months of worsening memory reported by her daughter. Which workup approach is MOST appropriate at first presentation?
options: Cognitive testing, reversible-cause screen (B12, TSH, FBE, UEC, LFT, calcium), and structural imaging where atypical or onset under 65 years
CT brain for every patient before any bloods
Diagnosis on MMSE score alone without bloods
No workup - dementia is untreatable
Neuropsychology testing before any other step
explanation: Dementia workup: confirm cognitive impairment (validated screen + collateral), exclude reversible contributors (B12, thyroid, metabolic), and image when presentation is atypical, early-onset or focal signs exist.
pearl: Always exclude the reversible B12 and thyroid mimics.
trap: Skipping bloods - the occasional treatable dementia.

stem: A 55-year-old man has a long-standing bilateral hand tremor worse when holding his coffee, a positive family history, and reduced tremor with alcohol. Examination otherwise normal. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Essential tremor
Parkinson disease
Functional tremor
Cerebellar disease
Hyperthyroidism
explanation: Bilateral action (postural) tremor with family history and alcohol responsiveness typifies essential tremor. Parkinson's tremor is rest tremor with bradykinesia/rigidity.
pearl: Action tremor + alcohol responsive + familial = essential.
trap: Reading bilateral tremor as early Parkinson's.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has 2 days of unilateral facial droop with incomplete eye closure and no forehead sparing. Ear examination, neurology and BP are normal. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Oral corticosteroids started now (within 72 hours of onset)
Aciclovir alone
No treatment - spontaneous recovery is the rule anyway
CT facial bones
Wait 72 hours to confirm it is not improving before steroids
explanation: Bell's palsy (lower motor neurone facial weakness including forehead) is treated with early oral corticosteroids within 72 hours to improve recovery; antivirals add little in idiopathic cases (add if Ramsay Hunt/zoster). Eye protection is mandatory.
pearl: Forehead involvement = LMN = Bell's; steroids early.
trap: Waiting to see - the steroid window closes at 72 hours.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with migraines now has a daily dull headache; she takes codeine-combination analgesics 20 days per month. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Withdraw the codeine analgesics with support and optimise migraine prophylaxis
Increase the codeine dose
Add a triptan daily
Switch to oxycodone for cleaner pain control
CT brain to exclude a new cause
explanation: Analgesic use ≥15 days/month for >3 months produces medication-overuse headache. Treatment is withdrawing the offending drug (with explanation, sometimes a bridging plan) and preventing migraines properly.
pearl: ≥15 analgesic days a month = the headache is the treatment.
trap: Escalating opioids, imaging the consequence not the cause.

stem: A 49-year-old woman develops a proximal DVT 2 weeks after a knee arthroscopy. It is her first VTE. What is the MOST appropriate anticoagulation duration?
options: 3 months, then stop (provoked by transient surgery)
Lifelong anticoagulation
12 months
Indefinite anticoagulation unless bleeding risk is high
6 months
explanation: VTE provoked by a major transient surgical risk factor is anticoagulated for 3 months; longer durations are for unprovoked, recurrent, or persistent-risk VTE.
pearl: Provoked by surgery: 3 months and out.
trap: Indefinite therapy for a clearly provoked event.

stem: A 58-year-old man has an unprovoked proximal DVT with no bleeding risk factors. What is the MOST appropriate approach to anticoagulation?
options: Anticoagulate for at least 3 months, then reassess the risk-benefit of continuing
3 months then always stop
Lifelong therapy without reassessment
Anticoagulate only if a thrombophilia is identified
No anticoagulation if he declines stockings
explanation: Unprovoked proximal VTE needs at least 3 months of anticoagulation followed by a documented reassessment (bleeding risk, patient preference, residual thrombosis/D-dimer where used) of continuing versus stopping.
pearl: Unprovoked VTE: 3 months minimum, then a deliberate decision.
trap: Automatic stopping at 3 months without the reassessment conversation.

stem: A routine blood test on a 70-year-old man shows WCC 62 with blasts on the film, Hb 92, platelets 40. He feels mildly tired but is afebrile. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Same-day haematology referral/hospital assessment
Repeat the FBE in 6 weeks
Oral iron and review
Antibiotics for presumed infection
Reassure - mild symptoms only
explanation: Leucocytosis with circulating blasts is a haematological emergency presentation requiring same-day haematology; watchful waiting risks leukostasis, bleeding and infection.
pearl: Blasts on film = today, not tomorrow.
trap: The well-looking patient defusing urgency.

stem: A 35-year-old vegetarian woman with iron deficiency (Hb 88, ferritin 5) develops nausea and constipation on oral iron despite taking it with food and alternate-day dosing. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Intravenous iron infusion
Continue oral iron indefinitely at the same dose
Stop all iron and transfuse
Iron injections daily
Diet alone given her intolerance
explanation: With failed or intolerant oral iron (and significant deficiency), IV iron (e.g., ferric carboxymaltose) is appropriate and repletes rapidly. Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise.
pearl: Oral iron failing or intolerant = IV iron, not willpower.
trap: Persisting for months with zero absorption or adherence.

stem: A 26-year-old woman of South-East Asian background has mild microcytosis (MCV 74) with normal haemoglobin and normal ferritin. What is the MOST likely explanation and next test?
options: Thalassaemia trait - haemoglobin electrophoresis (HbA2)
Iron deficiency - start iron
Anaemia of chronic disease - investigate inflammation
Lead toxicity
No testing needed
explanation: Microcytosis with normal Hb and normal ferritin in a high-prevalence ethnicity suggests thalassaemia trait; confirm with haemoglobinopathy studies (raised HbA2 in beta trait). Iron is not indicated.
pearl: Low MCV + normal ferritin = think thalassaemia before iron.
trap: Reflex iron therapy for every microcytosis.
